content: The 2013 guidelines for verifying measles elimination in the Western Pacific Region, published by the World Health Organization (WHO), provide a comprehensive framework for assessing progress toward the elimination of measles. These guidelines include definitions, principles, criteria, and evidence required for verification, as well as the roles and responsibilities of various verification committees. Key Definitions: 1. Measles Elimination: The verified interruption of measles virus transmission in a defined geographical area (e.g., a country or region) for at least 12 months, supported by a well-performing surveillance system. 2. Endemic Measles Transmission: Continuous transmission of indigenous or imported measles virus persisting for 12 months or more in a specific geographical area. 3. Endemic Measles Case: A laboratory-confirmed or epidemiologically linked case resulting from endemic transmission of the measles virus. 4. Re-establishment of Endemic Transmission: Occurs when a chain of measles virus transmission persists uninterrupted for 12 months or more in a previously measles-free area. 5. Measles Outbreak in an Elimination Setting: A single laboratory-confirmed case of measles. 6. Suspected Measles Case: A patient with fever and a maculopapular rash, with or without cough, coryza, or conjunctivitis, or a case suspected by a healthcare worker. 7. Laboratory-Confirmed Measles Case: A suspected case confirmed by a proficient laboratory. 8. Non-Measles, Non-Rubella Case: A suspected case discarded as neither measles nor rubella based on laboratory testing or epidemiological linkage to another confirmed communicable disease. 9. Measles Vaccine-Associated Rash Illness: A rash illness meeting specific criteria, including onset 7–14 days after vaccination, absence of respiratory symptoms, and no secondary cases identified. 10. Imported Measles Case: A case exposed to measles outside the region or country during the 7–21 days before rash onset. 11. Import-Related Measles Case: A locally acquired infection linked to an imported case, supported by epidemiological or virological evidence. 12. Unknown Source Measles Case: A confirmed case with no established epidemiological or virological link to importation or endemic transmission after thorough investigation. Verification Criteria: 1. Documentation of the interruption of endemic measles virus transmission for at least 36 months from the last known endemic case. 2. Presence of a verification-standard surveillance system. 3. Genotyping evidence supporting the interruption of endemic transmission. Lines of Evidence: 1. Detailed epidemiological description of measles since the introduction of the measles vaccine (and rubella vaccine, if applicable) in the national immunization program. 2. Quality of epidemiological and laboratory surveillance systems for measles. 3. Population immunity data, including birth cohort analysis and evidence related to marginalized and migrant groups. 4. Sustainability of the national immunization program, including resources for mass campaigns where appropriate. 5. Genotyping evidence supporting the interruption of measles virus transmission. Progress in the Western Pacific Region: Since the goal of measles elimination was established in 2003, the Western Pacific Region has made significant progress, reducing measles cases by 93% between 2008 and 2012. By the end of 2012, endemic measles virus transmission may have been interrupted in as many as 33 countries and areas, including the 21 Pacific island countries and areas considered as one epidemiological block. Reported coverage of the first dose of measles-containing vaccine (MCV1) reached 96% in 2011, and 33 countries and areas have introduced a routine second dose (MCV2), with reported coverage of 91%. Over 300 million children were vaccinated during large-scale supplementary immunization activities (SIAs) from 2003 to 2012. Surveillance and Laboratory Network: All countries and areas in the region conduct case-based, laboratory-supported surveillance for measles. Surveillance indicators, such as completeness and timeliness of monthly reporting, have improved significantly since 2007. The regional measles and rubella laboratory network includes 383 laboratories, with one WHO global specialized laboratory (GSL) in Japan, three regional reference laboratories (RRLs) in Australia, China, and Hong Kong (China), and 17 fully functional national measles-rubella laboratories (NMLs). Verification Mechanisms: Independent regional and national verification committees (RVCs and NVCs) oversee the verification process. RVCs and NVCs ensure the development of annual progress reports and coordinate submissions to verify progress toward measles elimination. Verification of national measles elimination and progress toward elimination is conducted annually until global measles eradication is achieved. Post-Verification Needs: Countries that have achieved measles elimination must maintain high levels of population immunity, verification-standard surveillance, and preparedness plans for outbreak response. These guidelines aim to support countries and areas in confirming measles elimination and provide guidance to those still working toward this goal.
